analysis.one_liner: Caps small short-term loans at roughly 36% interest and limits borrowers to a set number per year.
analysis.headline: The bill limiting repeat payday loans was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in April 2010 and never received a hearing, a vote, or a floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped lenders from making short-term, small-dollar loans — the typical payday loan — at annual percentage rates above 36% (or, for some open-end credit, where first-91-day costs exceed 25% of the credit line). It would also have barred a lender from giving a borrower more than six such loans in a year, or any loan running 90 days or longer, which is how payday borrowers get trapped paying fees on the same debt repeatedly. It required lenders to offer extended repayment plans, banned prepayment penalties, let state attorneys general enforce the rules, and let states keep stricter laws of their own.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who take out small, high-rate short-term loans — typically workers living paycheck to paycheck facing an emergency expense. The bill would cap the total cost of those loans, limit how many times a year a lender could extend one, require affordable extended repayment plans, and bar fees for paying early, so a borrower could not be charged fees indefinitely on the same $300 debt. Consumers in states with no payday protections of their own would gain the most, since the federal floor applies everywhere.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Payday borrowers stuck in repeat-loan cycles

how_it_helps.text: It bars lenders from making a sixth short-term, high-rate loan to the same borrower within a year, breaking the cycle of rolling loans over.
It defines the loans by total cost — fees, renewal charges, and credit insurance all count toward the 36% cap — so lenders cannot repackage the same cost as a 'fee' rather than interest.

It would require lenders to offer extended repayment plans when a borrower cannot pay, prohibit prepayment penalties, ban selling other products at payday loan locations, and let state attorneys general enforce the rules.
It voids contracts made in violation of the law and expressly lets states impose stricter protections of their own.

analysis.who_pays: Payday lenders and other issuers of small short-term loans, who would lose the high-fee, high-renewal business model the bill targets. Some borrowers would also lose access to this form of emergency credit if lenders stopped offering it rather than operate at a 36% cap.

drawbacks.text: By cutting off access to high-rate short-term credit, the bill could leave some borrowers with no source of emergency cash at all, since mainstream lenders do not make small, fast, unsecured loans at 36% APR.
The bill did not cover overdraft services or pawn transactions, so some of the most expensive forms of short-term credit would have remained outside its limits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to repeated payday borrowers is real: the 36% cap and the six-loan limit attack the debt-trap cycle directly, and the bill let states go further. The cost is that some borrowers who rely on payday loans in emergencies would lose access to that credit, since lenders cannot profitably make 91-day loans at 36% APR; critics argue this pushes borrowers to unregulated or offshore lenders or overdrafts (the bill left overdraft services uncovered). The unenforceability provision and state enforcement gave it teeth, but the bill never advanced far enough for these tradeoffs to be tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee in April 2010, and the committee never acted on it, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Kay Hagan introduced the Payday Lending Limitation Act of 2010 on April 22, 2010, with Senators Durbin and Schumer.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the same day.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, and no companion House action before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
The bill drew only two cosponsors, both Senate Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday lenders, who kept charging triple-digit rates on repeat short-term loans, were better off because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Payday lenders kept the status quo

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 22, 2010 and took no recorded action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Payday lending industry
against.what_they_did: Actively opposed federal restrictions on payday lending during this period, arguing the products serve borrowers banks turn away.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists; its supporters were Democrats, and no Republican cosponsor signed on.

industries.note: The bill caps their effective rates near 36% APR and limits how many loans they can roll over per borrower per year, cutting off their core business model of repeated fee-generating renewals. Payday lending is profitable precisely because rates far exceed 36%.

industries.industry: Banks and other small-dollar consumer lenders
industries.note: The bill reaches any lender making short-term loans of $3,000 or less above 36% APR, so banks and installment lenders offering similar products would face the same limits. Some might gain customers if payday lenders exit.
